- If SMSS > 1095 bytes and SMSS ≤ 2190 bytes: IW = 3 * SMSS bytes (maximum 3 segments)
- If SMSS ≤ 1095 bytes: IW = 4 * SMSS bytes (maximum 4 segments)

runs.query: What is false sharing, and why does it slow down multicore code?

legacy.answer:
False sharing is a performance problem that arises when two processor cores operate on independent data that happens to occupy the same cache line [1]. A cache line is the smallest unit of data that the caching system manages, typically 64 bytes [2].

Here's why it slows things down: when core A writes to its data on a shared cache line, the cache coherence protocol (like MESI on x86) forces it to invalidate that cache line on all other cores [2]. When core B then tries to access its own independent data on the same line, it finds its copy invalidated and must fetch the entire line again from cache or memory [2]. This happens repeatedly as the cores write, creating what amounts to serialized access despite the code appearing parallel [2].

The performance impact is dramatic. In a benchmark where two threads each increment their own counter 100 million times, false sharing caused a roughly 20-fold slowdown compared to a version where each counter occupied its own cache line [2]. The same computation, same threads, but vastly different performance based solely on data layout. More generally, eliminating false sharing can yield order-of-magnitude performance improvements [1].

The problem is particularly insidious because the code is logically correct: each thread only touches its own data with no actual data races [2]. Standard correctness tools will not catch it. Yet at the hardware level, the two cores are forced to run nearly serially because they keep invalidating each other's cache copies [2].

Mitigation typically involves padding or aligning data structures so that each thread's frequently written data occupies its own cache line, preventing multiple cores from sharing the same line [1].

Here's why it causes slowdowns. Modern CPUs cache memory in fixed-size lines, typically 64 bytes [2]. The cache coherence protocol (such as MESI on x86 systems) maintains consistency by invalidating a cache line across all cores whenever any core modifies it [2]. The problem occurs when two cores write to logically independent variables that share a cache line. Even though the cores are operating on unrelated data, the hardware cannot distinguish between them at the granularity of the cache line. When core A writes to its variable, it invalidates the cache line in core B's cache. Core B must then fetch the line again before it can proceed [2]. This "invalidate and re-fetch" cycle forces the cores to run serially in effect, despite appearing to run in parallel [2].

The performance impact is severe. A real-world example with two threads, each incrementing its own counter 100 million times with no logical sharing, ran roughly 18 to 20 times slower when both counters packed into the same cache line, compared to padding them to separate cache lines [2]. The problem is particularly insidious because the code is logically correct and contains no data races; only performance profilers reveal the issue [2].

Mitigation strategies include reordering variables, adding padding (unused bytes) between variables to separate them across cache lines, or using alignment attributes like alignas(64) [1, 2].

False sharing is a performance problem that occurs when multiple processor cores operate on independent data that happens to occupy the same cache line [1]. The caching system is unaware of the distinction between the data items and treats them as a single shared resource, even though the threads are logically accessing completely separate variables [2].

Here's why it causes slowdowns. Cache lines are the minimum unit of coherence in multicore systems, typically 64 bytes [2]. When one core writes to its data, the cache coherence protocol (such as MESI on x86) invalidates the same cache line on all other cores that hold a copy of it [2]. Those cores then must fetch the updated line from memory or another core's cache before they can proceed. If two cores are constantly writing to different variables on the same cache line, they trigger this invalidate-and-refetch cycle repeatedly, forcing them to run serially in effect despite appearing parallel [2].

The performance impact can be severe. In a typical benchmark where two threads each independently increment their own counter 100 million times, false sharing can cause a slowdown of around 15 to 20 times compared to code where each counter occupies its own cache line [2]. Another measurement showed that on an Intel Core i7 12th generation system, concurrent access with false sharing required about 50 times more computing time than with mitigation [1].

The problem is particularly insidious because the code is logically correct, contains no data races, and looks perfectly parallel [2]. Standard correctness tools will not detect it. The only practical fix is to ensure that frequently accessed variables used by different threads are separated onto different cache lines, typically through alignment or padding [1].
